title: Mandibular nerve (CN V3) injury with jaw deviation: exits skull via foramen ovale
vignette: A 26-year-old previously healthy man is brought to the emergency department following a motorbike accident. He is found to have a maxillofacial injury. His condition is stabilized, and surgical repair is performed. While recovering, the patient develops difficulty chewing food. On examination, the jaw deviates to the right side when the patient is instructed to open his mouth. The nerve that has been injured in this patient exits the skull through which of the following foramina?

clues.note: The muscles of MASTICATION (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).

clues.text: jaw deviates to the right side when the patient is instructed to open his mouth
clues.note: On opening, the lateral pterygoids protrude the jaw; unilateral CN V3 injury weakens that side, so the mandible DEVIATES TOWARD the injured (right) side - localizing to right CN V3.

whatMatters: Difficulty chewing with jaw DEVIATION TOWARD the injured side = MANDIBULAR nerve (CN V3) injury (motor to the muscles of mastication). CN V3 exits the skull through the FORAMEN OVALE. Answer B.
strategy: Localize to CN V3 (mastication + jaw deviation toward the lesion from lateral pterygoid weakness), then recall its exit: FORAMEN OVALE (mnemonic 'standing room only': V2 = rotundum, V3 = ovale). Reject other foramina/contents: foramen rotundum (CN V2 maxillary), foramen spinosum (middle meningeal artery), foramen lacerum (small vessels; ICA runs above it), and jugular foramen (CN IX, X, XI).

eliminations.label: Foramen lacerum - small vessels (ICA above it)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a cartilage-filled foramen transmitting small vessels; the internal carotid artery runs along its superior surface but does not traverse it. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: no trigeminal division passes through it. ✅ Correct if: asking about the internal carotid canal relationship.

eliminations.label: Foramen rotundum - CN V2 (maxillary)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: passage for the maxillary division (CN V2). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: V2 is sensory to the midface; this patient has a MOTOR/mastication (V3) deficit. ✅ Correct if: maxillary (V2) sensory loss.

eliminations.label: Foramen spinosum - middle meningeal artery
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: transmits the middle meningeal artery/vein and the meningeal branch of V3. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the main V3 trunk exits via the foramen OVALE, not spinosum. ✅ Correct if: middle meningeal artery (epidural hematoma).

eliminations.label: Jugular foramen - CN IX, X, XI
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: passage for glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves (and jugular vein). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: none of these control mastication; V3 uses the foramen ovale. ✅ Correct if: CN IX-XI deficits.

reasoning: Difficulty chewing implicates the muscles of mastication (CN V3)
Jaw deviation toward the right on opening = right lateral pterygoid weakness (right CN V3 injury)
The mandibular division (CN V3) exits the skull through the foramen ovale
mechanism: The TRIGEMINAL nerve (CN V) has three divisions exiting the skull through separate openings: OPHTHALMIC (V1) via the SUPERIOR ORBITAL FISSURE, MAXILLARY (V2) via the FORAMEN ROTUNDUM, and MANDIBULAR (V3) via the FORAMEN OVALE (mnemonic: 'Standing Room Only' - Superior orbital fissure, Rotundum, Ovale for V1, V2, V3). V3 is the only division with a MOTOR component, supplying the MUSCLES OF MASTICATION: three jaw-CLOSERS (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) and the jaw-OPENER/protruder (lateral pterygoid). On OPENING, the lateral pterygoids protrude/depress the mandible; with UNILATERAL V3 injury the affected lateral pterygoid is weak, so the intact (contralateral) muscle pushes the jaw TOWARD the injured side (jaw deviates TOWARD the lesion). Bilateral injury causes jaw drop. Thus difficulty chewing with jaw deviation to the right localizes to the RIGHT mandibular nerve, which exits via the foramen ovale. The foramen ovale also transmits the lesser petrosal nerve, accessory meningeal artery, and emissary veins. The distractors transmit other structures (V2, middle meningeal artery, small vessels, CN IX-XI).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > trigeminal nerve & skull foramina: V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale ('Standing Room Only'); V3 = only motor division (muscles of mastication); jaw deviates TOWARD the injured side; foramen spinosum = middle meningeal artery.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Mastication weakness + jaw deviation toward lesion = CN V3 -> foramen ovale.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on CN V3/mandibular nerve, muscles of mastication, lateral pterygoid, foramen ovale, or 'Standing Room Only'? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Rotundum = V2; spinosum = middle meningeal artery; lacerum = small vessels; jugular foramen = CN IX-XI.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale; jaw deviates toward the injured V3 side.

keywords.back: V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 rotundum, V3 ovale

keywords.front: Jaw deviation with unilateral V3 injury
keywords.back: Toward the injured side (weak lateral pterygoid)

firstAid.detail: Anatomy: mastication; exits foramen ovale; jaw deviates toward lesion.
Anatomy > V1 SOF, V2 rotundum, V3 ovale.

memoryHook: Chewing runs on V3, and V3 drops out of the skull through the foramen OVALE (Standing Room Only: V1, V2, V3 = fissure, Rotundum, Ovale); a weak jaw swings toward the hurt side.
